summary: For ages 5–6, learners read and write the number words one–twenty and connect each word to its numeral and its quantity (a three-way word↔numeral↔quantity mapping with a spelling/production component). Many number words are irregular sight words (one, two, eight, twelve). Some teen words are opaque ('eleven' and 'twelve' give no clue to ten-and-one or ten-and-two), and others say the ones-part first ('thir-teen', 'fif-teen'), so teaching should keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached while building sight-word recognition and correct spelling. Practise both reading (word→quantity) and writing (numeral→word) directions. A wider 0–20 reference range (washing line, chart) can support this, while the production target is the words one–twenty.
misconceptions: Reading a number word as text without linking it to a quantity or numeral.
Spelling confusions: four/for, eight, nine→'nighn', and the many silent/irregular letters.
Teen/decade word muddles by sound: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty'.
Assuming all number words are phonically regular and mis-decoding the irregular ones (one, two, eight).
Reversing the teen meaning because the word says the ones first (thir-teen → thinking 3 then 1 → 31).

activities.title: Word–numeral–quantity triple match
steps: Hear or read a number word such as 'thirteen'.
Place or drag that word card onto its numeral (13).
Place it onto a ten-frame or set showing one full ten plus three.
Match across the number words one–twenty (with 0–20 available as reference), including a playful pairs/memory game over the words.
Also work the reverse direction: given a numeral or a quantity, find and say the matching word.
activities.insight: The number word carries meaning: it names a specific numeral AND a specific quantity, so the word must be read for meaning, not just decoded as text.

activities.title: Build-the-word: spell the number for a numeral
steps: Look at a shown numeral (for example 13).
Use letter tiles, tracing, or handwriting to build or write the matching word ('thirteen').
Check the spelling against a reference wall, correcting classic traps like four/for and thirteen/thirty.
Spell several words one–twenty, returning to the irregular and teen forms for extra practice.
activities.insight: Reading a number word and producing its correct written form are different skills; learners need to spell the word, not only recognise it.

activities.title: Teen zone: keep ten-and-ones visible
steps: Segment each teen word from thirteen to nineteen beside its quantity: thir·teen, four·teen, fif·teen, and so on.
Place each segmented word next to a ten-frame showing one full ten plus the ones part.
Memorise 'eleven' and 'twelve' as sight words paired with their ten-and-ones frames.
Say the word slowly and match it to the quantity, noticing that the ones-word comes first (thir-) but the quantity is ten-and-three.
activities.insight: The teens name ten-and-ones even though the word is opaque ('eleven'/'twelve') or says the ones-part first; keeping the structure visible helps prevent the reversal 'thir-teen → 31'.

activities.title: Number words in real reading and writing
steps: Read a short real instruction, e.g. 'buy twelve eggs', and set out that many counters, then write the numeral.
Label a box of 15 crayons with the number WORD.
Meet number words on a washing line 0–20, on classroom labels, and in books/rhymes repeatedly, not just in a maths drill.
Read a word to make or point to the quantity, and write the word for a given numeral.
activities.insight: Number words are used to act in the world: reading one to do something and producing a word label shows real command beyond reciting.

activities.title: Reference wall: tap-to-hear number words 0–20
steps: Use a 0–20 chart showing each numeral, its word, and a matching quantity.
Tap an entry to hear the word spoken and see the teen structure highlighted.
Return to the wall to check spelling and meaning while reading or writing elsewhere.
activities.insight: A consistent reference linking numeral, word and quantity supports recall of sight words and teen structure during other tasks.

checkQuestion: Give a real task. 'This shopping list says buy twelve eggs — read it and put out that many counters, then write the numeral.' Then: 'Label this box of 15 crayons with the number WORD.' Watch them read a number word to act, and produce the word form.
checkAnswer: Reads 'twelve' and sets out 12, writes 12; labels the box 'fifteen'. Uses the word correctly in the task, not just recites it.
